title: Same shape means same answer
weak_claim: These two pictures are the same topologically, so the answer is the same for the original problem, even though the sentence has not named which moves preserved the object, boundary data, or rule. The weak wording is attractive because it sounds like a summary, but it leaves out the part that would let a reader check the claim. A better version starts by saying exactly what thing is being studied and what kind of evidence the sentence is allowed to use.
why_weak: The sentence skips the object and the permission. A reader cannot tell whether the gluing rule, endpoint data, boundary order, or forbidden crossing rule survived the move. Same under what rule is the whole question; without that rule, the phrase same topologically can hide a changed problem. This matters outside topology too: a model, count, diagram, or source can look persuasive while answering the wrong question. The point is not to make the wording longer; it is to stop the sentence from promising more than the object, theorem, picture, model, or source can carry.
first_principles_repair: Say what the object is first. Then say the picture was changed only by moves that keep the gluing rule, boundary data, and forbidden regions fixed, so the question being answered is still the original question. The repaired sentence makes the legal route visible before the simplified endpoint is trusted. The repair earns the larger lesson by showing why the detail matters before asking the reader to remember a name. A reader can remove the formal term and still understand the chain from object to condition to evidence to conclusion.
detail_to_check: Check one local move at a time and ask whether it changes the rule that defines the object, not whether the final drawing looks cleaner. If one step moves fixed data, crosses forbidden matter, or changes an identification rule, the final picture no longer speaks for the starting one. The check matters because it turns understanding into a repeatable act, not a memory of a phrase. The check has to use everyday words first, then any formal name that helps shorten the finished account.
where_to_use: Use this repair on deformation, quotient, knot, route, and surface pages before saying that a simplified drawing proves the original claim. It belongs wherever sameness is asserted from a cleaner picture. The course connection to deformation, quotient-space, topology-vs-geometry is strongest when the reader can see the same repair habit in a fresh problem. This is also the bridge to applications: the same repair prevents overclaiming when topology ideas are used to talk about motion, data, networks, physical systems, or source evidence.

title: The count is invariant
weak_claim: This number is invariant, so it proves the obstruction and shows the desired motion cannot happen, even before the page checks which local changes are allowed and why the number survives them. The missing piece is not decoration; it is the reason the sentence would still be true after the picture, model, or source trail is tested. A better version starts by saying exactly what thing is being studied and what kind of evidence the sentence is allowed to use.
why_weak: The word invariant does all the work without naming the allowed changes or explaining why the number survives them. A reader can repeat the label while still not knowing why this count is allowed to travel from one drawing to another. The weakness is practical, not stylistic. It blocks the reader from knowing what to inspect next. The point is not to make the wording longer; it is to stop the sentence from promising more than the object, theorem, picture, model, or source can carry.
first_principles_repair: Name the moves the problem allows, then explain what happens to the count under each move. If new pieces appear in matched pairs, or if signed contributions cancel, say that plainly before using the number as evidence. The repair also says what conclusion the surviving number is strong enough to force. The safest version tells the reader what survives, what threatens it, and what conclusion follows because it survived. A reader can remove the formal term and still understand the chain from object to condition to evidence to conclusion.
detail_to_check: Ask what event could change the raw count and what rule prevents that event from changing the protected count. If the answer cannot describe one threatening local event, the invariant claim is probably only a name. Use the check to decide whether the sentence needs a weaker conclusion or an added condition. The check has to use everyday words first, then any formal name that helps shorten the finished account.
where_to_use: Use this repair on Euler characteristic, parity, winding, linking, intersection-number, and graph-planarity explanations whenever a number is used as proof. It fits any page where a count travels across drawings. The related concepts are invariant, intersection-number, euler-characteristic, but the repaired claim must explain their work before naming them. This is also the bridge to applications: the same repair prevents overclaiming when topology ideas are used to talk about motion, data, networks, physical systems, or source evidence.

title: The theorem applies
weak_claim: By the theorem, the required point or obstruction exists, so the example has the conclusion we wanted before the theorem's contract, hypotheses, object, current setting, and conclusion type are checked. A reader needs to know whether the sentence is about a surface, a path, a field, a count, a source, or a physical state. A better version starts by saying exactly what thing is being studied and what kind of evidence the sentence is allowed to use.
why_weak: The sentence asks the theorem to speak before proving that the current object is the kind of object the theorem is about. It also hides the limit of the theorem's conclusion, so existence can slide into construction or a total count can slide into a solved motion path. A stronger explanation must tell the reader which detail carries the force of the argument and which detail is only background. The point is not to make the wording longer; it is to stop the sentence from promising more than the object, theorem, picture, model, or source can carry.
first_principles_repair: Before the theorem name, list the object, the rule or field on it, the needed condition, and the exact conclusion type. Then say whether the theorem gives existence, equality, parity, obstruction, or a count. The repaired sentence makes the theorem sound narrower but more trustworthy. This is the plain-language standard for the course: no term stands in for an object, a rule, or an evidence check. A reader can remove the formal term and still understand the chain from object to condition to evidence to conclusion.
detail_to_check: Check that the rule maps the space back into itself, the field includes all defects, or the surface/count is the one named by the theorem. Then check the conclusion limit: what does the theorem not locate, compute, or construct? The detail is part of the idea, because it says what the idea can safely be used to do. The check has to use everyday words first, then any formal name that helps shorten the finished account.
where_to_use: Use this repair on fixed-point, Brouwer, Poincare-Hopf, vector-field index, and theorem-contract pages whenever a theorem name appears before its object and conditions. It also belongs in answer guides. Use brouwer-fixed-point, poincare-hopf, fixed-points as labels for completed checks, not as replacements for the checks. This is also the bridge to applications: the same repair prevents overclaiming when topology ideas are used to talk about motion, data, networks, physical systems, or source evidence.

first_principles_repair: Point to the exact feature being used: a side change, a forced crossing, a signed pair, a boundary order, a hole in a state space, or a whole-surface total. A reader can remove the formal term and still understand the chain from object to condition to evidence to conclusion.
detail_to_check: Ask whether redrawing the picture, changing scale, or moving a curve legally would keep the named feature. Use the check to decide whether the sentence needs a weaker conclusion or an added condition. The check has to use everyday words first, then any formal name that helps shorten the finished account.

title: The model captures the motion
weak_claim: The configuration space shows whether the system can move from one physical position to another before one state, the forbidden states, and the translation back to physical motion are named. The repair begins by replacing the label with the everyday job the label performs in this exact problem. A better version starts by saying exactly what thing is being studied and what kind of evidence the sentence is allowed to use.
why_weak: The sentence skips the meaning of one point in the model and does not say which physical states were removed as impossible. It treats the diagram as if topology can inspect motion before the model has earned its connection to the physical system. The reader needs the missing condition because the condition is what separates a useful idea from a loose association. The point is not to make the wording longer; it is to stop the sentence from promising more than the object, theorem, picture, model, or source can carry.
first_principles_repair: Say what one point of the configuration space records: every position, angle, choice, or relation needed for one allowed state. Then name the collision, boundary, or blocked states that have been removed. The repaired sentence also states what kind of conclusion the model can support: a route exists, a route is blocked, or a special state is forced. The repaired wording works in topology first, then travels to another field only after the same model contract is rebuilt. A reader can remove the formal term and still understand the chain from object to condition to evidence to conclusion.
detail_to_check: Trace one physical motion and one path in the state space, and confirm that every intermediate point represents a legal physical state. Also check the reverse: every modeled path used in the proof translates back to a motion the system could actually make. That distinction keeps the page from treating every kind of support as if it proved the same strength of claim. The check has to use everyday words first, then any formal name that helps shorten the finished account.
where_to_use: Use this repair on configuration-space, product-space, motion-family, and transfer-lab pages whenever a physical story is turned into a path question. It fits any modeled motion claim. In another field, the matching repair is to name the model state, allowed change, protected measurement, and claim limit before borrowing configuration-space, product-space, deformation. This is also the bridge to applications: the same repair prevents overclaiming when topology ideas are used to talk about motion, data, networks, physical systems, or source evidence.

title: Signs cancel
weak_claim: The plus and minus terms cancel, so the signed total, not the raw count, carries the final answer without explaining the shared sign convention, comparable assignments, or the local cancellation event. The missing piece is not decoration; it is the reason the sentence would still be true after the picture, model, or source trail is tested. A better version starts by saying exactly what thing is being studied and what kind of evidence the sentence is allowed to use.
why_weak: The sentence treats signs as if they were automatic labels. It does not explain where the shared direction rule comes from or why opposite signs are comparable. A plus and a minus can cancel only after the page earns a common sign convention. The weakness is practical, not stylistic. It blocks the reader from knowing what to inspect next. The point is not to make the wording longer; it is to stop the sentence from promising more than the object, theorem, picture, model, or source can carry.
first_principles_repair: Name the orientation rule, boundary direction, or local direction comparison that assigns signs. Then explain the local pair creation or cancellation event that keeps the signed total stable. The repaired sentence makes cancellation a checked event, not an arithmetic wish. The safest version tells the reader what survives, what threatens it, and what conclusion follows because it survived. A reader can remove the formal term and still understand the chain from object to condition to evidence to conclusion.
detail_to_check: Ask whether a plus sign in one place and a minus sign in another place were assigned by the same rulebook. If the rule cannot be carried across the object, the signed total may not be defined. Use the check to decide whether the sentence needs a weaker conclusion or an added condition. The check has to use everyday words first, then any formal name that helps shorten the finished account.
where_to_use: Use this repair on boundary orientation, intersection number, vector-field index, and formula-reader pages whenever cancellation is used as evidence. It belongs wherever signs do mathematical work across one object. The related concepts are boundary-orientation, intersection-number, vector-field-index, but the repaired claim must explain their work before naming them. This is also the bridge to applications: the same repair prevents overclaiming when topology ideas are used to talk about motion, data, networks, physical systems, or source evidence.

title: Local behavior determines the whole surface
weak_claim: The local pieces add up to the global conclusion, so the whole surface must obey the formula even before the complete account, boundary terms, hidden defects, and surface identity are checked. The broad phrase hides the work that matters: naming what is being protected and what change would stop protecting it. A better version starts by saying exactly what thing is being studied and what kind of evidence the sentence is allowed to use.
why_weak: The sentence says local and global without explaining the bookkeeping bridge between small neighborhoods and the whole object. It names the direction of the argument but not the mechanism that carries local facts into a surface-wide conclusion. The sentence becomes teachable only when the failure case is visible enough that the reader can avoid it later. The point is not to make the wording longer; it is to stop the sentence from promising more than the object, theorem, picture, model, or source can carry.
first_principles_repair: Describe one local contribution first, such as a turn, defect index, angle shortage, or cell piece. Then explain the rule for adding all contributions across the whole surface and what total they must match. The repaired sentence says why no isolated patch is enough by itself. Then add the limit: what the sentence does not prove, locate, compute, construct, or justify from the available evidence. A reader can remove the formal term and still understand the chain from object to condition to evidence to conclusion.
detail_to_check: Ask whether every local contribution is included exactly once and whether the surface used for the total is the same surface being studied. Missing a boundary term, hidden defect, or glued edge can make the global conclusion belong to the wrong object. If that check cannot be performed, the sentence is not ready to appear as a course principle. The check has to use everyday words first, then any formal name that helps shorten the finished account.
where_to_use: Use this repair on Gauss-Bonnet, Poincare-Hopf, Euler characteristic, triangulation, and local-to-global theme pages when local evidence is summed. It fits any argument that adds local contributions. The same habit transfers beyond topology only when the new field has its own object, rule, and evidence named as clearly as gauss-bonnet, poincare-hopf, euler-characteristic require here. This is also the bridge to applications: the same repair prevents overclaiming when topology ideas are used to talk about motion, data, networks, physical systems, or source evidence.

title: Topology is only about shape
